To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the concept of organizational legitimacy, as a way of analysing corporate behaviour, is supported, but that (ii) the concept of the political economy of accounting, as a way in which corporate behaviour can be analysed, is also supported.
‘executives perceive a degree of social responsibility, but are not always clear about the extent to which this is imposed on them, or whether it is a matter of their own choosing’.

the executives interviewed perceived that their company had an obligation to act in a socially responsible manner, but that they also perceived that their company was in a strong position to influence the views of the various interest groups to whom it was accountable.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the extent to which the executives of large, UK businesses perceive themselves to be accountable to, and/or to be able to influence the expectations of, the various societal interest groups with whom their companies interact.
the attitudes towards perceived social responsibility of a small sample (n=8) of large, UK based companies.
the nature of perceived corporate accountability, and the extent to which this is perceived to relate to the views of various societal interest groups.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, whilst the organizational legitimacy perspective may appear more valid in the short-term, the political economy of accounting perspective may be more appropriate in the longer-term.
both perspectives have some validity in explaining corporate behaviour, and that it is impossible to say which perspective is more important.

the executives of the sample companies appear to perceive their organizations as being accountable for the social responsibility of their actions, but that this does not necessarily preclude the possibility that their behaviour is also being proactively managed, in an attempt at agenda-setting, to influence societal expectations in a favourable direction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there is evidence that executives are aware of the need for organizations to be perceived as socially responsible, but that there is a degree of cynicism as to the extent of the social responsibility of the organization, and a degree of scepticism as to the ability of the company to be able to influence societal expectations.

the concept of organizational legitimacy is a useful way of examining the perceived social responsibilities of large, UK businesses, although the extent to which the executives of these businesses are able to manipulate the views of their stakeholders is also an important consideration.

there are some indications that executives perceive a need for corporate social responsibility, although this is not necessarily a result of societal expectations, but rather an attempt to ‘set the corporate agenda’ in such a way as to manipulate societal views of corporate actions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the executives interviewed appear to perceive that their organizations are accountable, and are attempting to manage expectations in the direction that they wish.
there is evidence to suggest that the concept of organizational legitimacy is a useful one, and that it is a view of corporate activity that is widely held by executives in the UK.
the executives we interviewed are clearly aware that they are accountable to a wide variety of stakeholders, and are concerned to manage their reputations accordingly.
